newsitem.title: ITALY: Poor turnout threatens Italy's referendums.
newsitem.headline: Poor turnout threatens Italy's referendums.

text.p: A referendum in which Italians were asked to vote on seven issues as diverse as hunting and privatisation was in doubt on Sunday amid indications that a majority of voters could stay away from polling stations.

Factors threatening to deny the exercise a quorum included voter fatigue after three general elections in five years, media indifference and sweltering heat that sent Italians flocking to the beaches.
For a referendum to be valid, more than 50 percent of Italy's 49 million eligible voters have to take part.

Only 13.2 percent had cast their ballots by five p.m. (1500 GMT), 10 hours after polling stations opened, according to official figures. Voting was to end at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT), with computer projections of the results expected soon after.

RAI Uno television, which reported the referendums low down on its lunchtime news bulletin, said the turnout by late afternoon was slightly below the level at a similar stage in 1990 referendums on hunting and the use of pesticides.
They were invalidated because only 43 percent of Italians took part, the only time since World War Two that a referendum has failed to secure a quorum.
Six of Sunday's referendums were championed by the minority Radical Party, whose leader Marco Pannella won his greatest triumph with a referendum in 1974 that legalised divorce.

It wanted to set new restrictions on the careers of magistrates, limit rights to hunting, scrap the Italian journalists' guild, make conscientious objection easier, and remove the right of the Treasury to retain a controlling "golden share" in strategic privatised industries.
The seventh referendum, proposed by some of Italy's regions, sought to abolish the Agriculture Ministry and decentralise responsibility for farms policy.
Critics argued that the seeming triviality of the issues and the high number of ballots would devalue the referendum as a weapon of popular democracy.
Referendums have proved a powerful tool to force legislative change in Italy since the early 1970s.
They have allowed the people to intervene on fundamental concerns that the country's ponderous parliament either cannot or will not tackle effectively.
Centre-left Prime Minister Romano Prodi said he would vote in the referendums but with a "certain sense of unease".
"The referendum is a great institution, the maximum in democracy...but you can't use it on technical problems whose significance people don't even understand," he said.

His line was contested by opposition leader and media magnate Silvio Berlusconi, the target in 1995 of a referendum that sought to limit his ownership of television stations. The attempt was defeated on the ballot.

"I hope all Italians realise that democracy is something important. You only notice it is missing and realise its importance when it isn't there," Berlusconi told reporters at a polling station in Milan.
Italy's first post-war referendum in 1947 abolished the monarchy in favour of a republic.
The country may face another crucial referendum in 1998 or 1999 on radical constitutional change now being discussed by parliamentarians to reform the workings of government and the state.
